title: Baselines, change control and configuration
blurb: Explain what a baseline is, why changing a baselined product needs authorization, and how records keep versions under control.
question: A product description was approved last month and the team now wants to alter it. Why can't the author just edit it, and what records keep the versions straight?

teach.body: The project baseline is the current approved versions of the management products and project products that are subject to change control. A change is a modification to any of those approved products. In plain English: once a product has been approved, it becomes the agreed reference point. Anyone can propose altering it, but nobody alters it without going through change control.

items.label: Request for change captured and assessed
Change approved: version 1.1 becomes the baseline

teach.caption: The baseline is always the CURRENT approved version, not the first one.

teach.h: What gets baselined, and at what level
teach.body: Approved management products such as the PID, the project plan and the management approaches are baselined, as are approved project products. When the board authorizes the project, the PID is baselined and later used to judge performance. The baselines guidance asks the project management team to decide the appropriate level at which products are baselined, and notes that each approved change creates a new version.

Plans, costs, timescales and the business case all rest on the baseline, so altering it can ripple through the project. Change control ensures each change is identified, assessed and then approved, rejected or deferred. A request for change must identify the products to be changed and the justification; if it has a cost, funding comes from the change budget or additional customer funding. Changes to the baselined PID found during lower-level planning also go through the issue management approach.

steps.label: Assess
steps.sub: impact on targets, business case, other products

teach.h: Records that keep versions under control
head: Record or practice
What it does
rows: Lists all products of a plan and their status
Holds formal issues, including requests for change
Record of changes plus archive of old versions
Actual status compared with authorized state
teach.caption: Baselines may sit in different systems, but each must keep a change record and an archive of superseded versions (manual 10.3.1).

teach.body: Ashcombe Regional Airport is upgrading its baggage hall. The signage product description was baselined at version 1.0. Operations manager Ruth Kemp requests larger signs, so project manager Elif Demir captures a request for change and assesses its cost. Once the change authority approves it, version 1.1 becomes the baseline and 1.0 is archived. Later, project support officer Owen Price checks the product register against what is installed and finds two signs still built to 1.0.

teach.text: Classic traps: the baseline is the CURRENT approved version, not the original one frozen at initiation. And the product register (all products of a plan and their status) is not the quality register (quality activities and their results).

items: Project baseline: the current approved versions of products subject to change control.
A change is a modification to any approved product that forms the baseline.
Decide the level at which products are baselined; each approved change creates a new version.
A request for change identifies the products to change and the justification; costs come from the change budget or extra customer funding.
Keep a record of changes and archive superseded versions; periodically check actual product status against the authorized state.

summary: You can now explain what the project baseline is and why a baselined product changes only through change control. You can also describe how the product register, configuration control and periodic status checks keep product versions under control.

A.q: Which term means the current approved versions of the management products and project products that are subject to change control?
options: Product register
Project log
Project baseline
Project plan
A.why: That is the definition of the project baseline (manual 10.1).

whyNot.0: The product register lists the products of a plan and their status; it is a record, not the baseline itself.
whyNot.1: The project log holds the daily log, lessons log and the issue, risk, quality and product registers.
whyNot.3: The project plan is one baselined product, not the whole set of approved products.

A.q: Which is the PRINCE2 7 definition of a change?
options: A modification to any approved product that forms the project baseline
An event relevant to the project that needs management consideration
A move of the organization from its current state to a target state
A product that will not meet the quality specifications agreed for it
A.why: A change is a modification to any of the approved products that constitute the project baseline (manual 10.1).

whyNot.1: That is the definition of an issue.
whyNot.2: That describes change management, part of the people element.

A.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. The baselines guidance advises periodically checking that the actual status of products matches their [?] state.
options: forecast
authorized
contracted
delivered
A.why: Good practice is to verify periodically that the actual status of products reflects their authorized state, looking for discrepancies (manual 10.2.1).

whyNot.0: A forecast is a prediction; the check compares reality with what has been authorized.
whyNot.2: A contract may set supply terms, but the check is against the authorized state of each product in the baseline.
whyNot.3: The delivered state is the actual status being checked, not the reference it is checked against.

B.q: Why should a change to a baselined product be authorized before it is made?
options: So the change management approach can plan training for each new version
So the quality register can record the change instead of the issue register
So the business layer can reset the project tolerances for each change
So its impact on targets, the business case and other products is assessed
B.why: Change control makes sure a change is identified and its impact assessed before it is approved, rejected or deferred, because plans and the business case rest on the baseline.

whyNot.0: The change management approach covers organizational transition, not version control of products.
whyNot.1: Requests for change are formal issues recorded in the issue register; the quality register records quality activities.
whyNot.2: Project tolerances are set by the business layer for the project as a whole, not reset for each change.

B.q: What must a request for change identify?
options: The products to be changed and the justification
The risk owner and the risk action owner
The quality method and reviewer for each product
The highlight report frequency and its audience
B.why: Under change control, a request for change must identify the products to be changed and the justification for the change (manual 10.2.3).

whyNot.1: Risk owners and risk action owners are risk register headings.
whyNot.2: Quality methods and reviewers are set out in product descriptions and the quality register.
whyNot.3: Reporting frequency is agreed through the communication management approach and the board.

B.q: A product has been changed three times since it was first approved. What should the system holding it provide?
options: A single current copy, with earlier versions removed
A new product description for each team member
A record of changes and an archive of old versions
An exception report for each change that was made
B.why: Each system holding baselines should enable configuration control by keeping a record of changes and an archive of superseded versions (manual 10.3.1).

whyNot.0: Superseded versions are archived, not removed, so the history of the product can be traced.
whyNot.1: One product description defines the product; the team does not need a copy each.
whyNot.3: Exception reports are for forecast breaches of stage or project tolerance, not for every change.

C.q: During initiation the PID is approved. Later, lower-level planning shows that part of it needs to change. When is the PID baselined, and how is the change handled?
options: When the project brief is approved; through the risk management approach
When the board authorizes the project; through the issue management approach
When the first stage ends; through the change management approach
When the project closes; through the quality management approach
C.why: The authorized PID is baselined when the board authorizes the project, and changes to the baselined PID arising from lower-level planning go through the issue management approach.

whyNot.0: The project brief is approved earlier, in starting up a project; the PID does not exist yet, and baseline changes are not handled by the risk approach.
whyNot.2: The PID is baselined at project authorization, and the change management approach covers organizational transition.
whyNot.3: The PID is used throughout the project, and changes to it are not handled through the quality management approach.

C.q: A periodic check compares the actual status of products with their authorized state. Which guidance area covers this check, and which record lists the products and their status?
options: Issue resolution; the daily log
Change budget; the risk register
Quality planning; the lessons log
Baselines; the product register
C.why: The baselines guidance advises periodically checking actual product status against the authorized state, and the product register lists the products of a plan and their status.

whyNot.0: Issue resolution is about judging what to record as an issue; the daily log is the PM's informal diary.
whyNot.1: The change budget funds approved changes; the risk register holds risks.
whyNot.2: Quality planning produces product descriptions and the quality approach; the lessons log holds lessons.

C.q: Which statement about baselines is correct?
options: Each approved change creates a new version that becomes the baseline
The baseline is the first approved version and stays fixed until closure
Draft products are part of the baseline from the moment work starts
Team managers alter baselined products at each checkpoint date
C.why: The baseline is the current approved versions; each approved change creates a new version, which becomes the new baseline.

whyNot.1: The baseline moves forward as changes are approved; it is not frozen at the first version.
whyNot.2: Only approved products form the baseline; drafts are not yet under change control.
whyNot.3: Baselined products change through change control, not at checkpoint dates.

reteach.title: The architect's drawings
reteach.question: Why can't a builder just redraw an approved architectural plan when the client asks for a bigger window?

blocks.body: Once the client signs off drawing revision A, it is the reference everyone builds to. If the client asks for a bigger window, the architect assesses the cost and structural impact, the client approves it, and revision B is issued. Revision A is kept in the archive, stamped 'superseded'. A site inspector periodically checks that what is built matches the current revision.

blocks.text: The baseline is the latest approved revision, not the first. Old revisions are archived, not thrown away.

explain.body: A product becomes part of the baseline when it is approved. From then on, altering it is a change, and changes go through change control.

test.q: A product description has just been approved. What is now true of it?
options: It can be revised freely by its author
It is owned by the business layer
It is subject to change control
It is recorded in the risk register
test.why: Approved products form the baseline and are subject to change control.

whyNot.0: Free revision is for drafts; an approved product changes through change control.
whyNot.1: Approval does not transfer ownership to the business layer.
whyNot.3: The risk register holds risks, not approved products.

explain.body: The project management team decides the appropriate level at which products are baselined: too detailed and change control becomes a burden, too coarse and changes slip through.

test.q: Under the baselines guidance, what should the project management team decide?
options: The risk appetite of the organization
The level at which products are baselined
The frequency of checkpoint reports
The benefits tolerance for the project
test.why: The baselines guidance asks the team to decide the appropriate level at which products need to be baselined (manual 10.2.1).

whyNot.0: Risk appetite is set by the business, not under the baselines guidance.
whyNot.2: Checkpoint frequency is set in the work package.
whyNot.3: Benefits tolerance is a progress and business case matter, set out in the benefits management approach.

explain.body: The product register in the project log lists all the products required of a plan and their status, which makes status checks and version control possible.

test.q: Which record lists all the products required by a plan, together with their status?
options: Quality register
Issue register
Lessons log
Product register
test.why: The product register lists all products required of a plan and their status.

whyNot.0: The quality register summarizes quality management activities and their results.
whyNot.1: The issue register holds formal issues.
whyNot.2: The lessons log is an informal repository of lessons.

explain.body: If an approved change has a cost, the funding must be identified: either the approved change budget or additional funding from the customer.

test.q: An approved request for change has a cost. Where should the funding come from?
options: The change budget or additional customer funding
The risk budget or the stage tolerance margin
The benefits tolerance or a business layer reserve
The team manager's contingency or work package fee
test.why: If a change has a cost, its funding comes from the approved change budget or additional funding from the customer (manual 10.2.3).

whyNot.1: The risk budget funds risk responses, and tolerance is not a funding source for changes.
whyNot.2: Benefits tolerance is a permitted range for benefits, not a source of money.
whyNot.3: Team managers do not fund changes to the baseline from their own work package.
